rationale: IBD is consistently linked to lower gut diversity, and genus-level relative abundances only show this indirectly. This version adds OTU-level alpha-diversity features to the random forest. Shannon, inverse Simpson and observed richness are computed after rarefying each sample to a common depth, so the large sequencing-depth differences between studies don't bias the diversity values.

Pooling four studies brings in large batch effects from sequencing depth, region and protocol. I'm adding a batch-corrected copy of each genus: its percentile rank within its own study, computed from all samples without using labels. The random forest can then compare samples against their study-mates while keeping the raw relative abundances.

Many IBD signals are clearest at the family level (loss of Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae, gain of Enterobacteriaceae/Pasteurellaceae), and lumping every unassigned genus into one `g__` bin throws that away. I'm adding family-level relative abundances and their within-study percentile ranks alongside the genus features, so these signals stay visible and are more robust when genus assignment varies by study or region.

Keep the random forest on its current features and average its probabilities 50/50 with an L2 logistic regression fit on CLR log-ratios. The CLR inputs are genus and family log-ratios, filtered to taxa present in at least 5% of samples and centered within each study. The regularization strength is picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold only. IBD dysbiosis is largely an additive shift in log-ratios (Faecalibacterium/Roseburia down, Enterobacteriaceae/Pasteurellaceae up), which a linear compositional model captures smoothly where the RF splits it into steps. Centering within each study removes per-study offsets from depth and protocol, so the two models should make different errors and the average should rank cases better.

Some of the strongest IBD signals show up above the family level: Proteobacteria expand, Firmicutes (Clostridia) are lost, and the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes balance shifts. These are also more stable across studies with different 16S regions and classification depth. Adding the family features helped, so this round adds phylum, class and order relative abundances, each with its within-study percentile rank, to extend the same taxonomy approach.

Pooling the studies gives hundreds of genus and family columns. Most are rare and present in only a few samples or one study. With `max_features='sqrt'` these noisy columns fill most of the candidate pool at each split and weaken the forest. This version keeps only taxa present in at least 5% of all samples. The filter uses no labels and runs before the raw and within-study rank views are built, so splits concentrate on prevalent taxa that are measured across studies.

I'm averaging the current random forest's probabilities with an ExtraTrees model trained on the same features. ExtraTrees picks split thresholds at random, which should give a smoother ranking over the within-study percentile and abundance features and make different errors from the RF, so the average should rank cases better on the noisy pooled multi-study data.

I'm adding a microbial dysbiosis index, the log ratio of IBD-expanded families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Gemellaceae) to depleted orders (Clostridiales, Bacteroidales, Erysipelotrichales). This index is published in Gevers 2014, one of the pooled studies. I add it raw and as a within-study percentile rank, alongside the log ratio of the butyrate producers Faecalibacterium and Roseburia. The forest can only build these ratios from many separate splits on noisy columns, while a single summary log ratio does not change with sequencing depth and should carry over better across studies.

Average the current random forest with a slow, heavily subsampled LightGBM trained on the same genus, family and within-study rank features, combining the two by rank. Boosting fits the residual errors the forest leaves behind, using small trees on random subsets of columns. That should model the steady shifts in dysbiotic taxa more finely than the forest's fully grown, independent trees, so its errors should differ more from the forest's than ExtraTrees' did in round 7.

The forest currently grows every tree until each leaf holds a single sample. On noisy pooled multi-study data, that makes each tree's vote close to 0/1, which hurts ranking and so AUROC. This round sets a minimum leaf size, chosen from {1, 3, 6, 12} by grouped inner CV on the training fold only. Larger leaves average labels over many samples, which should give smoother and better-ranked probabilities.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between the four pooled studies. The forest can only infer which study a sample came from indirectly, through hundreds of noisy batch-shifted abundance columns, and with `max_features='sqrt'` those columns are rarely in the candidate set together. This version adds one explicit covariate: each study's smoothed case rate, estimated from the training fold's labels inside `fit_predict` only, so it is label-safe. The forest gets the study-level prior directly and can spend its splits on within-study microbial differences.

Use control-referenced percentile normalization (Gibbons et al. 2018), which was designed for pooled case-control microbiome studies. Inside `fit_predict`, each genus and family abundance is converted to its percentile among the training-fold controls of the same study, and these features are added to the forest's existing inputs. The current label-free within-study ranks shift with each study's case/control ratio, so the same rank means different things in different studies. Ranking against each study's own healthy controls puts every study on the same "deviation from healthy" scale. For any study with fewer than 5 training controls, the existing all-sample within-study rank is used instead.

AUROC depends on how finely the probabilities rank samples. With hundreds of noisy genus, family and rank columns and `max_features='sqrt'`, a 500-tree forest gives coarse vote fractions that vary with which columns each tree happened to sample. Raising the forest to 2000 trees reduces that Monte Carlo variance and gives smoother, more stable rankings. Everything else stays the same, including the features, split rules and the fact that no hyperparameters are tuned.
